story.headline: Wall Street's slide in AI stocks deepened, pulling US yields down sharply and trimming bets on a December Fed hike. The yen gained most, while the Aussie and gold fell further.

reads.policy: A December Fed hike is still expected, but bets slipped as stocks fell and US consumers said they expect less inflation. The European Central Bank, Bank of England and Bank of Japan are also expected to hike in December. A softer Fed path would narrow the US rate lead that has carried the dollar.
reads.growth: A deep slide in US tech stocks is now a worry for growth in its own right, since falling share prices can make households and companies spend less. US consumers stayed gloomy in November. Commodity currencies like the Aussie and kiwi feel growth fears first.
reads.inflation: US consumers now expect noticeably less inflation over the next year than they did a month ago, which takes a little pressure off the Fed. Inflation is still above target almost everywhere, so most central banks still lean toward hikes. Japan's prices stayed above the Bank of Japan's goal, keeping a December hike there likely.
reads.risk: US stocks fell for a seventh day as the sell-off in AI companies deepened, with Nvidia down sharply on a report that a regulator is looking at its accounting. Money ran into the yen and US government bonds, and a gauge of market nerves hit its highest since March. The Aussie and kiwi fell, as they usually do when stocks slide.
reads.tot: Gold fell to its lowest in about 14 months, which weighs on the Aussie. Oil bounced on new attacks in the Gulf but still fell for a third week, which takes support away from the Canadian dollar.
reads.positioning: The latest weekly figures show hedge funds leaning toward the dollar and the pound and against the euro, the kiwi and the Canadian dollar, with bets against the kiwi growing fastest. Big long-term investors take the other side on the euro, pound and Aussie. Where the two groups disagree, a surprise could set off a fast unwind.
reads.fiscal: France's debts, flagged by the European Central Bank as a risk, keep weighing on the euro. US long-term borrowing costs slipped back below 5% as money ran to safety, but record US government borrowing still weighs a little on trust in the dollar.

fed.summary: The Federal Reserve held rates on October 28 with two officials voting to hike, and most officials now expect more hikes. A deeper US stock slide and cooler inflation expectations trimmed December bets a little, but a hike is still the likely next move.
fed.priced: December: hike very likely, though a little less certain after the stock slide. More hikes expected next year.
fed.why: US inflation is running at about twice the Fed's 2% goal. US consumers now expect prices to rise more slowly, and a falling stock market gives officials a reason to go carefully.
fed.watch: Whether the stock slide keeps going and changes how officials talk, and US business surveys on Monday, November 23. The decision is December 9.

boc.summary: The Bank of Canada raised rates to 2.50% in October and said more may be needed. October inflation held at 3.1% with core prices near 2%, so a December hike now looks less likely than not.
boc.priced: December: hold more likely, with a hike a bit under even odds.
boc.why: Energy is lifting headline inflation, but core prices are calm and the economy is shedding jobs, so the bank can afford to wait.
boc.watch: Oil prices, which fell sharply this week, and Canada's November jobs figures on December 4. The decision is December 9.

rbnz.summary: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand held at 2.75% in October in a narrow vote. Rising unemployment has made a December hike less certain, and the kiwi has fallen to its lowest since 2020.
rbnz.priced: December: hike possible but not fully expected.
rbnz.why: Inflation pressures argue for a hike, but unemployment at its highest since 2015 argues for waiting. Governor Anna Breman gave no clear signal on December in her latest speech.
rbnz.watch: The official election result on November 27 and the next dairy price auction. The decision is December 9.

ecb.summary: The European Central Bank held at 2.50% in October and a December hike is widely expected. Euro-area inflation is confirmed at 4.0%, but the euro sits just under $1.10 as US rates rise faster.
ecb.priced: December: hike widely expected, possibly the last for a while.
ecb.why: Euro-area inflation is about double the bank's goal and core prices are firming. Weak factories and France's debts, which the bank's stability report singled out, limit how far it can go.
ecb.watch: Euro-area business surveys for November next week. The decision is December 17.

boj.summary: The Bank of Japan holds at 1.25%, far below other major banks, and is expected to hike in December. Japan's October inflation came in a touch below forecast but stayed above the bank's 2% goal, which keeps that hike likely.
boj.why: Inflation has stayed above 2% for a second month, and the weak yen keeps pushing up import and food prices. The small summer contraction is the main reason to wait.
boj.watch: Any sign Japan steps in to buy yen if the dollar nears 160 again, and Governor Kazuo Ueda's next comments. The decision is December 18.

rba.summary: The Reserve Bank of Australia raised rates to 4.85% on November 3, the highest among the major banks. Australia lost jobs in October and unemployment hit a five-year high, which supports the view that rates have peaked, and the Aussie is near its lowest in a year.
rba.priced: December: a hold expected. Some bets on cuts in 2027 are building.
rba.why: Inflation is still too high for most of the board, but the job market is clearly weakening. That makes a further hike unlikely and puts the timing of a first cut in question.
rba.watch: Any comment from Governor Michele Bullock on the jobs figures, and gold prices. The decision is December 8.

boe.summary: The Bank of England raised Bank Rate to 4.00% on November 5 and said more may follow. UK shoppers spent more than expected in October, which supports a second hike in December, but the pound sits near its lowest this year as US rates rise faster.
boe.priced: December: a second hike more likely than not.
boe.why: High fuel costs from the Middle East conflict keep UK inflation near twice the bank's goal. Spending held up in October, although much of it was food stockpiling that may not last.
boe.watch: UK business surveys for November next week, after retail sales beat forecasts in October. The decision is December 17.

snb.summary: The Swiss National Bank holds its rate at zero and can sell francs if they get too strong. Low Swiss inflation means no hike is in sight.
snb.why: Swiss inflation is low, so the bank has no reason to raise rates and some room to cut if the franc climbs.
snb.watch: Any flare-up that sends money into the franc. The decision is December 10.

GBP.summary: The pound sits at the top of the board because UK interest rates are among the highest of the eight. Strong UK shopping in October helps, but it is still near its lowest this year as the global stock slide weighs on it.

AUD.summary: The Aussie sits second on the board, thanks to the highest interest rates among the major central banks. But Australia's October job losses suggest those rates have peaked, and a global stock slide and falling gold pushed it to its weakest in about a year.

USD.summary: The dollar sits third on the board. High US interest rates support it, while large budget deficits weigh a little. It held near its highest since April 2025 even as a stock slide pulled US yields lower.

NZD.summary: The kiwi sits fourth, in the middle of the board. Firm prices for New Zealand's dairy exports help, but a global stock slide keeps it close to its lowest since 2020.

EUR.summary: The euro sits fifth, just below the middle of the board. Cheaper oil helps the euro area, but France's debts and rates below most of the others hold it back. It sits just under $1.10, not far from its weakest in about 18 months.

CAD.summary: The Canadian dollar sits sixth, in the lower half of the board. Falling oil prices hurt Canada's exports, and recent Canadian data has mostly missed forecasts. It is near its weakest against the US dollar in more than a year.

JPY.summary: The yen sits second from the bottom because Japanese interest rates are far below the others. A global stock slide and a likely December Bank of Japan hike made it the strongest of the eight on Friday, November 20, pulling the dollar back from just under 160 yen.

CHF.summary: The franc sits at the bottom of the board. Swiss interest rates are the lowest of the eight and inflation is too low to need higher rates. A global stock slide sent safe-haven money into it, pulling the dollar off an 18-month high.
